newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish show small nations can tackle big EU issues.
newsitem.headline: Irish show small nations can tackle big EU issues.

text.p: Ireland hands over the stewardship of the European Union to the Netherlands on January 1 after a presidency remarkable for the scale of its achievements and for the size of the challenge it leaves behind.
For six months some of the biggest tests facing Europe were shouldered by one of its smallest countries.

Ireland proved equal to the task. It took the 15-nation bloc giant strides forward on the road to a single currency and laid the foundations for a new treaty to prepare for an influx of new members and take the EU into the 21st century.
The Dublin summit in mid-December won Ireland glowing praise from across the EU and heralded a new optimism that Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would take place on time.
"Dublin has shown all past scepticism to be wrong," said European Commission President Jacques Santer. "It has shown what political determination, perseverence and optimism can achieve."

But Ireland sidestepped some of the most thorny issues facing the EU, like the balance of power between large and small states and rules for flexible integration which would allow more enthusiastic countries to integrate faster than the rest.

It will be up to the Dutch to try to bridge the gaps between member states on these divisive issues by the Amsterdam summit in June -- the deadline the EU has set itself for adoption of its new treaty.
Analysts say the crowning achievement of Ireland's presidency was the creation of an economic and legal framework for Europe's proposed single currency, the euro.

Most importantly, a deal was finally brokered on December 13 on a "stability pact" to ensure fiscal discipline among EMU participants, after marathon negotiations to resolve disagreements between France and Germany.

On the same day the proposed designs for euro banknotes were unveiled. Critical acclaim was muted -- British Chancellor Kenneth Clarke said the "psychedelic" designs were "alright". Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring called them "interesting" -- but they provided a tangible sign that the euro is on the way.

EU diplomats say that if agreement had not been reached, the Dublin summit would have been seen as the moment when the single currency project began to unravel. Instead, the Irish presidency brought the euro ever closer to reality.
"We achieved all our goals for EMU and perhaps exceeded even our own expectations," a senior Irish diplomat told Reuters.
He said Ireland was also proud of its work in advancing the inter-governmental conference (IGC), the EU's review of the way it works which is due to lead to a new treaty in June.

"We take particular satisfaction from having chaired the IGC and having brought it from a preliminary stage to a point where we now have a substantial draft treaty," the diplomat said. "It has been widely accepted as a positive basis for future work."
Although the draft was unaminously accepted at December's Dublin summit, it left out the two most controversial issues -- flexible integration and the institutions of an enlarged EU.
Agreement will be extremely difficult to reach on these issues, particularly due to Britain's suspicion of further integration, analysts say. The Dutch face an uphill struggle.

"We brought the treaty a long way towards fruition," the diplomat said. "We were never going to finish it -- that wasn't our objective. The remaining issues will be difficult nuts to crack, but our draft provides a textual focus for negotiations."

France has criticised Ireland's draft, saying it should have been far more ambitious. But EU diplomats say Ireland's aim was to produce an outline that would be accepted by all, postponing the inevitable arguments until later.

Despite the work still to be done, diplomats in Brussels say Ireland's presidency was one of the most successful of recent times. Ireland says its success proves that small nations have a major contribution to make to the EU.

Smaller states fear their influence may wane as the bloc prepares for the entry of new members. Some suspect they may lose their right to nominate a commissioner or take their turn holding the presidency.

But the presidencies of Ireland and Belgium have won acclaim from EU diplomats in Brussels, while the most recent French, Italian and German presidencies are widely viewed as less satisfactory. Ireland hopes its success will strike a blow for the rights of Europe's minnows.

"Undoubtedly one of the lessons to be learned from this presidency is that even though it imposes an enormous strain, a small administration like ours is capable of rising to the challenge and acquitting ourselves not just adequately, but extremely well," the Irish diplomat said.
